content: Teeth are present in the oral cavities of humans and numerous other animals. The term teeth is the plural form of tooth. Teeth exhibit a variety of shapes, sizes, and lengths. In adult humans, there are typically 32 teeth, which play a crucial role in the mastication of food. The outermost layer of teeth is covered by a hard, protective substance known as enamel. Proper care is essential when cleaning or brushing teeth to maintain their health and functionality. Well-maintained teeth not only serve a functional purpose but also contribute to an aesthetically pleasing appearance. The term tooth is defined as a hard, calcified structure located in the mouths of many vertebrate animals, primarily used for eating. Mammals exhibit a specific arrangement of teeth, including incisors, canines, premolars, and molars. This dental pattern is unique to mammals and their evolutionary ancestors, although the number and types of teeth vary significantly across species. Zoologists utilize a standardized dental formula to describe the specific arrangement of teeth in different groups. Human teeth are small, calcified, hard, whitish structures found in the mouth. They function to mechanically break down food by cutting and crushing it, preparing it for swallowing and digestion. The roots of teeth are embedded in the maxilla (upper jaw) or mandible (lower jaw) and are covered by gingiva (gums). Teeth are composed of multiple tissues with varying densities and hardness. In cetaceans, such as whales, the teeth have unique features. Whale teeth possess polyp-like protrusions on the root surface, composed of cementum. In humans, these protrusions are located on the external root surface, whereas in whales, they are found inside the pulp chamber. Human teeth have cementum on the outer root surface, while whale teeth are entirely covered in cementum, with a thin enamel layer only at the tip, visible in older whales where the cementum has worn away. The molar tooth of the woolly mammoth (Mammuthus primigenius) is an example of a lophodont cheek molar. A specimen collected in Estonia in 2006 and added to a collection in 2008 demonstrates the unique dental morphology of this extinct species. Sahelanthropus tchadensis, one of the oldest known species in the human evolutionary lineage, lived approximately 7 to 6 million years ago in West-Central Africa (Chad). This species exhibited a combination of ape-like and human-like features. Ape-like traits included a small brain, sloping face, prominent brow ridges, and elongated skull. Human-like traits included small canine teeth, a short mid-face, and a forward-positioned foramen magnum, indicating an upright posture and bipedal locomotion. Fossils of Sahelanthropus, including nine cranial specimens, were discovered in Chad in 2001, expanding the known geographic range of early humans beyond East and South Africa. Orrorin tugenensis, another early human species, lived around 6 million years ago in central Kenya. These individuals were chimpanzee-sized, with small teeth and thick enamel similar to modern humans. Fossil evidence, including an upper femur, suggests that Orrorin tugenensis was capable of both tree climbing and upright walking. This species is the only known member of the genus Orrorin. Adult horses typically have between 36 and 44 teeth. Their enamel and dentin layers are intertwined. Horses possess 12 premolars, 12 molars, and 12 incisors. Most male horses also have four canine teeth (tushes), while fewer than 28% of female horses have canines, and those that do often have only one or two, which may be partially erupted. Some horses have one to four vestigial premolars, known as wolf teeth, which are more common in the upper jaw and can interfere with the horse's bit. These teeth are often removed to prevent issues. Baboons produce vocalizations that include vowel-like sounds, such as grunts, wahoos, barks, yaks, and mating calls. These sounds suggest that the physical capacity for speech may have evolved over a longer timescale than previously thought. The baboon tongue has musculature similar to that of humans, with movements along two main axes enabling the production of vowel-like sounds. Anatomical studies show that the baboon tongue resembles that of a human child in shape and proportions. This evidence supports the idea that the ability to articulate vowel-like sounds, essential for human speech, may have been shared by the last common ancestor of humans and baboons approximately 25 million years ago. In dogs, the high pH of saliva reduces the likelihood of dental caries (cavities) by preventing enamel demineralization. Canine teeth, also known as cuspids, are pointed and used for tearing and grasping food. Many rodents, such as voles and guinea pigs, as well as lagomorphs like rabbits, have continuously growing molars in addition to incisors. In cartilaginous fish like sharks, teeth are attached to the jaw by tough ligaments rather than being embedded in bone. Teeth are believed to have first evolved in sharks and are absent in more primitive jawless fish. Structures resembling teeth in lampreys are composed of keratin rather than dentine or enamel and are unrelated to true teeth. Modern tooth-like structures with dentine and enamel have been found in late conodonts, but these are thought to have evolved independently of vertebrate teeth. The genes involved in mammalian tooth development are homologous to those responsible for fish scale development. Fossil evidence from the extinct fish Romundina stellina shows that teeth and scales share the same tissues, supporting the theory that teeth evolved as a modification of scales. The genetic variant rs17032907 and the haplotype (ACA) of CA VI may be associated with susceptibility to dental caries. The IGF-1 (insulin-like growth factor 1) protein, which regulates growth and development, plays a role in the metabolism of hard dental tissues. IGF-1 and its receptor (IGF-1R) are involved in the late stages of tooth development and pulp differentiation. Tumor necrosis factor-alpha (TNF-α) is implicated in inflammatory processes, including periodontitis. TNF-α suppresses cementoblast differentiation and induces apoptosis, affecting cementum production. Various signaling pathways, such as p53, p38, Erk1/2, JNK, PI3K-Akt, and NF-κB, are activated during this process, with p53 playing a central role in mediating these effects. Teeth are common fossils found in many geological strata. The prehistoric period spans from approximately 7 million years ago to about 7,000 years ago. The teeth of Tyrannosaurus rex are believed to share a genetic origin with those of the sea perch (Tautogolabrus adspersus).
